q: Read the passage (Q31–Q35): "Handwriting by pen on paper engages multiple neural circuits linked to memory, attention, and fine motor control that rapid typing rarely activates. Recent classroom studies reveal that students who summarize lectures in their own handwritten notes recall conceptual relationships far better than peers who transcribe lectures verbatim on laptops. Digital devices remain invaluable for research and editing, yet abandoning handwriting entirely carries a quiet cognitive cost. A balanced classroom therefore pairs digital efficiency with the deliberate slowness of pen and paper." What is the central idea of the passage?
o: Laptops should be permanently banned from modern classrooms
Combining handwriting with digital tools offers the best cognitive and practical balance for learners
Typing verbatim improves conceptual memory more than summarizing by hand
Pen and paper are more efficient than digital devices for research and editing
e:
The passage highlights the cognitive advantages of handwriting while recognizing the research/editing value of digital tools, recommending a balanced classroom combining both.
Options A, C, and D exaggerate or contradict the text.

q: Based on the passage (Q31–Q35), the word "verbatim" most nearly means:
o: Word for word, exactly as spoken
e:
"Verbatim" means in exactly the same words as originally used—contrasted in the passage with summarizing in one's own words.
Summarizing requires deeper cognitive processing than verbatim transcription.

q: According to the passage (Q31–Q35), what advantage do digital devices retain for students?
o: Stronger fine motor control during writing
High value for research and editing
e:
The third sentence explicitly states: "Digital devices remain invaluable for research and editing."
The other three options describe advantages of handwriting.

q: What is the author's tone in the passage (Q31–Q35)?
e:
The author cites classroom studies objectively and advocates a balanced integration of both handwriting and digital tools.
There is no hostility or sarcasm.

q: Choose the most suitable title for the passage (Q31–Q35):
o: How to Type Faster in Lectures
Pen and Screen: Finding Balance in the Classroom
e:
"Pen and Screen: Finding Balance in the Classroom" accurately captures both elements compared and the author's balanced conclusion.
The other choices are off-topic.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: "She plays _____ violin beautifully, though she bought _____ inexpensive bow yesterday."
e:
The definite article "the" is used before musical instruments when referring to playing them ("plays the violin").
"Inexpensive" begins with a vowel sound /ɪ/, so it takes "an".

q: Fill in the blank with the correct tense form: "By the time the ambulance arrived, the injured cyclist _____ consciousness."
e:
When two actions occurred in the past, the earlier completed action ("had lost") takes the Past Perfect Tense, while the later action ("arrived") takes Simple Past.
Pattern: Past Perfect + before/by the time + Simple Past.

q: Choose the correct verb: "Neither the captain nor the players _____ willing to postpone the match."
e:
With "neither...nor" / "either...or", the verb agrees with the NEARER subject ("the players" — plural), requiring the plural verb "were".
If reversed ("Neither the players nor the captain"), it would take "was".

q: Fill in the blank with the appropriate preposition: "The new teacher is very proficient _____ spoken Sanskrit."
e:
The adjective "proficient" always takes the fixed preposition "in" ("proficient in a skill/language").
Similarly: "adept in/at", "versed in", "deficient in".

q: Change into Passive Voice: "The gardener waters the roses every morning."
o: The roses were watered by the gardener every morning.
The roses are being watered by the gardener every morning.
The roses have been watered by the gardener every morning.
The roses are watered by the gardener every morning.
e:
Simple Present Active ("waters") converts to Simple Present Passive: is/am/are + Past Participle ("are watered").
Time adverbial "every morning" stays unchanged.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said to me, "The earth revolves round the sun."
o: He told me that the earth revolved round the sun.
He told me that the earth had revolved round the sun.
He asked me if the earth revolves round the sun.
He told me that the earth revolves round the sun.
e:
Universal truths, scientific facts, and proverbs do NOT change tense in Indirect Speech even when the reporting verb ("said") is in the past tense.
"Said to me" becomes "told me".

q: Identify the CORRECTLY spelt word:
e:
"Accommodation" contains double 'c' and double 'm' (a-c-c-o-m-m-o-d-a-t-i-o-n).
It is one of the most frequently tested spelling words in UP TGT English.

q: Choose the closest SYNONYM of the word "Benevolent":
e:
"Benevolent" (Latin bene = well + volens = wishing) means well-meaning, charitable, and kind-hearted.
Its antonym is "malevolent".

q: What does the idiom "to burn the midnight oil" mean?
o: To work or study late into the night
e:
"To burn the midnight oil" means to read, study, or work diligently late into the night.
It originates from the era when scholars studied by oil lamps.

q: Spot the error: "Each of the students (A) / were asked to bring (B) / his own dictionary to the lab (C) / No error (D)."
o: his own dictionary to the lab
e:
"Each of + plural noun" takes a SINGULAR verb ("was asked"), not plural "were asked".
Correct sentence: "Each of the students was asked to bring his own dictionary to the lab."

q: Fill in the blank accurately: "Dr. Verma _____ in this university _____ 2018."
e:
An action that started at a definite point in the past (2018) and continues into the present takes Present Perfect Continuous ("has been teaching") + "since" (point of time).
"For" is used with a period/duration of time (e.g., "for eight years").

q: Choose the correct verb form: "The novelist, along with his three editors, _____ attending the book launch tonight."
e:
When a singular subject ("The novelist") is joined to another noun by "along with", "as well as", "together with", or "in addition to", the verb agrees with the FIRST subject ("is").
Parenthetical additions do not make a singular subject plural.

q: Fill in the blanks with the correct prepositions: "He was accused _____ theft, but later acquitted _____ all charges."
e:
Both "accused" and "acquitted" take the fixed preposition "of" ("accused of theft", "acquitted of charges").
Similarly: "convicted of", "guilty of", "deprived of".

q: Choose the phrasal verb that best replaces the italicized phrase: "Because of heavy rain, the organizers decided to *postpone* the open-air concert."
e:
"Put off" means to postpone or defer to a later date.
"Call off" means to cancel completely; "put out" means to extinguish (fire); "give up" means to surrender/quit.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said to him, "Have you completed the manuscript?"
o: She asked him that if he had completed the manuscript.
She asked him whether he has completed the manuscript.
She asked him whether he had completed the manuscript.
She told him if he completed the manuscript.
e:
Yes/No questions take "asked" + "if/whether" (never "that if"), shift Present Perfect ("have completed") to Past Perfect ("had completed"), and drop the question mark in assertive word order.
Thus B is completely accurate.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The doctor said to the patient, "Do not skip your evening dose."
o: The doctor advised the patient not to skip his evening dose.
The doctor advised the patient to not skip his evening dose.
The doctor forbade the patient not to skip his evening dose.
The doctor told the patient that he should not skipped his dose.
e:
Negative imperatives convert to "advised/ordered/requested + object + not to + V₁" ("not to skip").
Option C is wrong because "forbade" is already negative and never takes "not" ("forbade the patient to skip" would be valid).

q: Convert into Passive Voice: "Who wrote 'Paradise Lost'?"
e:
In formal grammar exams, "Who + V₂ + Object?" converts to "By whom + was/were + Object + V₃?" ("By whom was 'Paradise Lost' written?").
Note the mandatory subject-auxiliary inversion ("was 'Paradise Lost'"), ruling out C.

q: Transform the following Simple sentence into a Complex sentence without altering its meaning: "He confessed his guilt."
o: He confessed and he was guilty.
He confessed that he was guilty.
He was guilty, so he confessed.
e:
Replacing the noun phrase "his guilt" with the subordinate noun clause "that he was guilty" converts the Simple sentence into a Complex sentence.
Options A and D are Compound sentences; C remains Simple.

q: Rewrite the sentence by removing "too" without changing its meaning: "The news is too good to be true."
o: The news is so good that it cannot be true.
The news is very good and it is true.
The news is so good that it can be true.
The news is too good that it cannot be true.
e:
Structure "too + adj + to + V₁" transforms into "so + adj + that + subject + cannot/could not + V₁".
Hence "The news is so good that it cannot be true."

q: Which sentence is punctuated CORRECTLY?
o: "Where are you going" asked the guard?
"Where are you going?", asked the guard.
"Where are you going?" asked the guard.
"Where are you going." asked the guard?
e:
When a direct quotation is a question, the question mark goes INSIDE the closing quotation marks, no extra comma is added after it, and the reporting clause ends with a full stop.
Hence B is exact.

q: Select the MISSPELT word among the following:
e:
The correct spelling is "Maintenance" (m-a-i-n-t-e-n-a-n-c-e), NOT "Maintainance".
"Bureaucracy", "Lieutenant", and "Questionnaire" are all spelt correctly.

q: Choose the most accurate ANTONYM of "Ephemeral":
e:
"Ephemeral" means lasting for a very short time (transitory/fleeting).
Its direct opposite is "Permanent" (or enduring/eternal).

q: A person who hates or distrusts humankind is called a:
e:
"Misanthrope" (Greek misein = hate + anthropos = mankind) means a hater of humankind.
Philanthropist = lover of mankind; Misogynist = hater of women; Mercenary = soldier fighting solely for money.

q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom "a white elephant":
o: A costly possession that is burdensome and of little practical use
A sudden stroke of good luck
e:
"A white elephant" refers to an expensive item or project that costs much to maintain while yielding little utility.
It derives from the Southeast Asian legend of kings gifting sacred albino elephants to courtiers to ruin them financially.

q: Identify the type of the italicized subordinate clause: "I know the village *where Tagore stayed during the monsoon*."
e:
The clause modifies the noun "village" (identifying which village), so it is an Adjective (Relative) Clause introduced by the relative adverb "where".
If the antecedent "the village" were omitted ("I know where Tagore stayed"), it would become a Noun Clause.

q: Complete the unreal conditional sentence correctly: "If I _____ a bird, I would fly across the Himalayas."
e:
Second Conditional (hypothetical/contrary-to-fact present condition) uses the past subjunctive "were" for all subjects ("If I were...", "If he were...") paired with "would + V₁".
"Was" is avoided in formal exam grammar for "If I were...".

q: Choose the correct pair of words: "The judge remained completely _____ during the trial, whereas the sleepy juror seemed _____ to the arguments."
e:
"Disinterested" means impartial, unbiased, and free from self-interest (ideal for a judge).
"Uninterested" means bored or lacking interest (fitting a sleepy juror).

q: Select the grammatically CORRECT inverted third-conditional sentence:
o: Had he worked harder, he would have passed the interview.
Had he worked harder, he would pass the interview.
Would he have worked harder, he had passed the interview.
If he would have worked harder, he would have passed the interview.
e:
Third Conditional ("If + Past Perfect, ... would have + V₃") can drop "if" by inverting the auxiliary "Had": "Had he worked harder, he would have passed..."
Never put "would have" in the "if"-clause (ruling out D).

q: Fill in the blank accurately: "It is high time we _____ steps to curb urban air pollution."
e:
Expressions like "It is time / It is high time / It is about time + subject" are ALWAYS followed by the Simple Past Tense (past subjunctive) to indicate an overdue action: "It is high time we took steps..."
When followed directly by an infinitive (no subject), use "to + V₁" ("It is high time to take steps").

q: Choose the correct pair of verbs: "A large number of rare manuscripts _____ been digitized, yet the number of active readers _____ steadily declining."
e:
"A (large) number of + plural noun" means "many" and takes a PLURAL verb ("have").
"The number of + plural noun" refers to a single numerical figure and takes a SINGULAR verb ("is").

q: Which of the following sentences uses the preposition after "die" INCORRECTLY?
o: He died of malaria during the expedition.
She died from overwork and exhaustion.
The brave soldier died for his motherland.
The old tree died with a fungal blight.
e:
Standard usage: "die of" (disease, hunger, thirst), "die from" (external cause like overwork, wound, overeating), "die for" (a noble cause/country), "die in" (battle/harness).
Option D misuses "with" instead of "of/from".

q: Identify the exact meaning of the phrasal verb "bear out" in the sentence: "The forensic report did not *bear out* the suspect's alibi."
e:
"Bear out" means to confirm, support, or corroborate a claim or testimony.
Compare: "bear with" = tolerate patiently; "bear down on" = press heavily toward.

q: Choose the correct Passive form of: "Quinine tastes bitter."
o: Quinine is bitter when it is tasted.
e:
Verbs of sensation (taste, smell, feel, read) followed by an adjective form a Quasi-Passive structure: "Subject + be + adjective + when + it/they + be + V₃" ("Quinine is bitter when it is tasted").
Similarly: "Honey tastes sweet" → "Honey is sweet when it is tasted."

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The old woman said to the prince, "May you live long and prosper!"
o: The old woman asked the prince if he might live long and prosper.
The old woman blessed the prince that he might live long and prosper.
The old woman said to the prince that he may live long and prosper.
The old woman exclaimed that the prince will live long and prosper.
e:
Optative sentences (wishes/prayers/blessings starting with "May") change "said to" into "wished/prayed/blessed", insert "that", and shift "may" to "might" in assertive order.
Hence B is exact.

q: Which of the following is the exact POSITIVE degree transformation of: "Very few Indian poets are as musical as Sarojini Naidu"? (Convert to Superlative)
o: Sarojini Naidu is the most musical Indian poet.
Sarojini Naidu is one of the most musical Indian poets.
Sarojini Naidu is more musical than all Indian poets.
No other Indian poet is as musical as Sarojini Naidu.
e:
"Very few + plural noun + are + as...as" corresponds to Superlative "one of the + superlative + plural noun" ("one of the most musical Indian poets") and Comparative "more...than most other".
"No other" (not "very few") corresponds to "the most musical".

q: Which sentence demonstrates the CORRECT use of a semicolon (;) between independent clauses?
o: Although the storm raged outside; the concert continued smoothly.
The experiment failed twice; nevertheless, the team refused to quit.
She packed three essentials; a compass, a lantern, and a map.
Because he was late; he missed the keynote address.
e:
A semicolon correctly links two closely related independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb ("nevertheless", "however", "therefore") followed by a comma.
Options A and D misuse a semicolon after a dependent clause; C requires a colon (:) before a list.

q: Identify the CORRECTLY spelt word:
e:
"Supersede" (meaning to replace or take the place of) is the ONLY English word ending in "-sede" (from Latin sedere = to sit).
Only three words end in "-ceed" (exceed, proceed, succeed), while the rest end in "-cede" (precede, recede, concede).

q: Choose the closest SYNONYM of "Perspicacious":
e:
"Perspicacious" (Latin perspicere = to look through) means having ready, sharp insight and acute mental discernment.
Do not confuse it with "perspicuous" (meaning clearly expressed / lucid).

q: A speech or piece of writing delivered in formal praise of someone who has recently died is called a/an:
e:
A "Eulogy" is a formal speech or tribute praising a deceased person (typically at a funeral).
An "Epitaph" is an inscription on a tombstone; an "Elegy" is a mournful poem; an "Epilogue" is a concluding section of a literary work.

q: What does the Latin literary/legal phrase "sine qua non" mean?
o: An indispensable condition or essential element
e:
"Sine qua non" literally means "without which not"—an absolutely essential condition without which something cannot exist.
Compare: "ex officio" (by virtue of office), "bona fide" (in good faith), "prima facie" (at first sight).

q: How many lines does a traditional sonnet contain, and what is the rhyme scheme of a Shakespearean (English) sonnet?
e:
A Shakespearean sonnet consists of 14 lines in iambic pentameter divided into three quatrains and a concluding rhyming couplet (abab cdcd efef gg).
Option B is the Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet (octave + sestet).

q: A mournful, reflective lyric poem written to lament the death of a particular person (such as Milton's *Lycidas* or Shelley's *Adonais*) is called a/an:
e:
An Elegy (especially a Pastoral Elegy) laments the dead and typically moves from grief to philosophical consolation.
An Ode is an elevated address; a Ballad is a narrative folk poem; a Satire ridicules folly or vice.

q: Identify the figure of speech in the line: "Parting is such *sweet sorrow*" (Shakespeare, *Romeo and Juliet*).
e:
An Oxymoron juxtaposes two contradictory or opposite terms side by side ("sweet sorrow", "open secret", "deafening silence") for sharp rhetorical effect.
Simile compares using "like/as"; Hyperbole exaggerates; Onomatopoeia imitates sound.

q: Which figure of speech is used in Wordsworth's famous line: "Ten thousand saw I at a glance, / Tossing their heads in sprightly dance"?
e:
"Ten thousand... at a glance" is Hyperbole (exaggeration for emphasis), while attributing "tossing their heads" and "sprightly dance" to daffodils is Personification.
Both devices vividly convey the poet's joyous awe.

q: Unrhymed iambic pentameter—used extensively by Shakespeare in his plays and by Milton in *Paradise Lost*—is known as:
e:
Blank Verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter (ten syllables per line, alternating unstressed and stressed beats), introduced into English by Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey.
Free Verse has neither regular metre nor regular rhyme; Heroic Couplet consists of rhymed iambic pentameter pairs.

q: Where was William Shakespeare born in April 1564, and what are his four 'Great Tragedies'?
o: Canterbury — *The Tempest*, *Twelfth Night*, *As You Like It*, *The Merchant of Venice*
London — *Romeo and Juliet*, *Julius Caesar*, *Titus Andronicus*, *Timon of Athens*
e: Shakespeare was baptized on 26 April 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon (Warwickshire). His four Great Tragedies—*Hamlet*, *Othello*, *King Lear*, and *Macbeth*—were famously studied by A. C. Bradley in *Shakespearean Tragedy* (1904).

q: In which Shakespearean play does the famous soliloquy "To be, or not to be: that is the question" appear?
e:
Prince Hamlet delivers the "To be, or not to be" soliloquy in Act III, Scene 1 of *Hamlet* (c. 1600–01), contemplating existence, suffering, and death.
*Macbeth* features "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" (Act V, Scene 5).

q: How many books does the final (1674) edition of John Milton's epic poem *Paradise Lost* contain?
e:
*Paradise Lost* was first published in 10 books in 1667 and revised into 12 books (on the Virgilian model of the *Aeneid*) in 1674.
Its stated purpose is to "justify the ways of God to men" (Book I, line 26).

q: In which year was *Lyrical Ballads*—jointly authored by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, marking the formal launch of English Romanticism—first published?
e:
*Lyrical Ballads* was published anonymously in 1798 (opening with Coleridge's *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* and closing with Wordsworth's *Tintern Abbey*).
Wordsworth added his famous critical Preface to the second edition in 1800 (expanded in 1802).

q: "A thing of beauty is a joy for ever" is the celebrated opening line of which poem by John Keats?
e:
"A thing of beauty is a joy for ever" opens Book I of Keats's poetic romance *Endymion* (1818), dedicated to the memory of Thomas Chatterton.
It encapsulates Keats's lifelong devotion to aesthetic beauty.

q: In which year was John Galsworthy awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, primarily for his monumental chronicle *The Forsyte Saga*?
e:
John Galsworthy (1867–1933) won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Literature "for his distinguished art of narration which takes its highest form in *The Forsyte Saga*."
He donated the entire prize money to the PEN Club, of which he was the first president (1921).

q: What was George Orwell's real birth name, and where in British India was he born in 1903?
e:
George Orwell was born Eric Arthur Blair on 25 June 1903 in Motihari (Bengal Presidency, now Bihar, India), where his father worked in the Opium Department.
He adopted the pen name "George Orwell" (after the River Orwell in Suffolk) in 1933.

q: Which allegorical novella by George Orwell (1945) satirizes the Russian Revolution and Stalinist totalitarianism through farm animals who declare "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others"?
e:
*Animal Farm* (1945) is Orwell's beast-fable allegory of Stalinism, featuring Old Major (Marx/Lenin), Napoleon (Stalin), Snowball (Trotsky), and Boxer (the loyal working class).
*Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949) is his dystopian novel of Big Brother and Oceania.

q: In Aristotle's *Poetics*, the purging or purification of the audience's emotions of pity and fear through watching a tragedy is termed:
e: Catharsis is the emotional cleansing/purgation of pity and fear; Hamartia = tragic flaw/error of judgment; Peripeteia = sudden reversal of fortune; Anagnorisis = moment of tragic recognition/discovery.

q: Which figure of speech substitutes a closely associated attribute or object for the thing itself—as in "The *pen* is mightier than the *sword*" or "The *Crown* has rejected the bill"?
e:
Metonymy replaces a concept with something closely associated with it ("pen" = writing/press, "sword" = military force, "Crown" = monarchy).
Synecdoche uses a physical PART for the whole (e.g., "all hands on deck" = sailors).

q: Who coined the critical term "Pathetic Fallacy" in *Modern Painters* (1856) to describe attributing human emotions to inanimate nature (e.g., "the cruel, crawling foam")?
e:
Victorian critic John Ruskin coined "Pathetic Fallacy" (from Greek pathos = feeling) in 1856.
T. S. Eliot coined "Objective Correlative" and "Dissociation of Sensibility"; Coleridge coined "Willing Suspension of Disbelief".

q: How many lines are in a 'Spenserian Stanza' (used by Edmund Spenser in *The Faerie Queene* and John Keats in *The Eve of St. Agnes*), and what is its concluding ninth line called?
e:
A Spenserian Stanza has 9 lines rhyming ababbcbcc: eight lines of iambic pentameter followed by a ninth line of iambic hexameter (12 syllables), called an Alexandrine.
Rhyme Royal (Chaucerian) has 7 lines (ababbcc); Ottava Rima has 8 lines (abababcc).

q: The first collected edition of William Shakespeare's 36 plays—known as the 'First Folio'—was published in 1623 by which two fellow actors of the King's Men?
e:
John Heminges and Henry Condell compiled and published the First Folio (1623), grouping 36 plays into Comedies, Histories, and Tragedies (*Pericles* was omitted).
Ben Jonson wrote the famous prefatory poem declaring Shakespeare "not of an age, but for all time!"

q: Which critic famously called Shakespeare an "upstart Crow, beautified with our feathers" in his 1592 pamphlet *Groats-Worth of Wit*?
e:
University Wit Robert Greene attacked the rising young playwright Shakespeare in 1592 as an "upstart Crow" and "the only Shake-scene in a country."
This provides the earliest surviving printed reference to Shakespeare's London theatre career.

q:
Match the following Shakespearean plays with their notable characters:
1. *The Tempest* — (a) Malvolio
2. *Twelfth Night* — (b) Prospero and Caliban
3. *The Merchant of Venice* — (c) Jaques and Rosalind
4. *As You Like It* — (d) Shylock and Portia
e: Correct matching: *The Tempest* — Prospero & Caliban (1-b); *Twelfth Night* — Malvolio (2-a); *The Merchant of Venice* — Shylock & Portia (3-d); *As You Like It* — Jaques ("All the world's a stage") & Rosalind (4-c).

q: John Milton's *Lycidas* (1637) is a celebrated pastoral elegy mourning the drowning of his Cambridge college friend:
e:
*Lycidas* (1637) laments Edward King, Milton's classmate at Christ's College, Cambridge, who drowned in the Irish Sea.
Compare: Tennyson's *In Memoriam* mourns Arthur Henry Hallam; Shelley's *Adonais* mourns John Keats; Spenser's *Astrophel* mourns Philip Sidney.

q: Which famous 1644 prose tract by John Milton is a passionate defence of the freedom of the press against pre-publication parliamentary licensing?
e:
*Areopagitica* (1644) opposes the Licensing Order of 1643, famously stating: "who kills a Man kills a reasonable creature... but he who destroys a good Booke, kills reason it selfe."
Its title echoes the Athenian court of the Areopagus.

q: "They also serve who only stand and wait" is the famous concluding line of which Milton sonnet?
o: *On His Having Arrived at the Age of Twenty-Three*
*On His Blindness* (*When I consider how my light is spent*)
e: Written after Milton became completely blind (1652), *On His Blindness* is a Petrarchan sonnet in which "Patience" reassures the poet that humble submission to God's will is itself true service.

q: In the *Preface to Lyrical Ballads* (1800), William Wordsworth defined poetry as:
o: "The spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity"
"A criticism of life under the conditions fixed for such a criticism by the laws of poetic truth"
"Not a turning loose of emotion, but an escape from emotion"
"The best words in the best order"
e:
Wordsworth gave the iconic Romantic definition of poetry in the 1800 Preface.
Compare: Matthew Arnold = "criticism of life" (B); T. S. Eliot = "escape from emotion" (C); S. T. Coleridge = "the best words in the best order" (D).

q: What is the subtitle of William Wordsworth's autobiographical blank-verse epic *The Prelude* (published posthumously in 1850)?
e:
*The Prelude; or, Growth of a Poet's Mind* (14 books in the 1850 version; addressed to Coleridge) traces Wordsworth's spiritual and imaginative development from childhood to poetic maturity.
His wife Mary Hutchinson gave the poem its title *The Prelude* after his death in 1850.

q: Which of John Keats's Great Odes of 1819 concludes with the famous enigmatic aphorism: "'Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know'"?
e: *Ode on a Grecian Urn* (1819) contrasts the permanence of art ("Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness") with fleeting human passion, concluding with the urn's message equating beauty and truth.

q: "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, / Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun" opens which celebrated ode by John Keats?
e: *To Autumn* (composed September 1819, three 11-line stanzas) is widely acclaimed as Keats's most serene and technically flawless ode, tracing autumn from ripeness to harvest to twilight song.

q: Which 1910 social problem play by John Galsworthy exposed the cruelty of solitary confinement in British prisons and prompted Home Secretary Winston Churchill to initiate prison reforms?
e:
*Justice* (1910), starring the weak clerk William Falder driven to forgery and ruined by prison solitary confinement, moved Winston Churchill to curtail solitary confinement rules in Britain.
*Strife* (1909) deals with capital vs. labour strike; *The Silver Box* (1906) exposes class bias in law; *Loyalties* (1922) tackles racial/social prejudice.

q: What is the title of the FIRST novel (1906) in John Galsworthy's celebrated trilogy *The Forsyte Saga*?
e:
*The Forsyte Saga* (1922 omnibus) comprises three novels—*The Man of Property* (1906), *In Chancery* (1920), and *To Let* (1921)—linked by two interludes (*Indian Summer of a Forsyte* and *Awakening*).
Soames Forsyte is the central "Man of Property."

q: In George Orwell's dystopian masterpiece *Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949), who is the protagonist working at the Ministry of Truth who secretly rebels against Big Brother?
e:
Winston Smith works in the Records Department of the Ministry of Truth (rewriting history in Oceania) and falls in love with Julia before being broken by O'Brien in Room 101.
John Flory is the protagonist of *Burmese Days* (1934).

q: In *Nineteen Eighty-Four*, which famous Party slogan is emblazoned on the facade of the Ministry of Truth?
o: "War is Peace. Freedom is Slavery. Ignorance is Strength."
e:
The three paradoxical slogans of Ingsoc ("War is Peace. Freedom is Slavery. Ignorance is Strength.") exemplify "Doublethink"—simultaneously holding two contradictory beliefs.
Option C is the sheep's chant in *Animal Farm*.

q: A strong rhythmic pause occurring near the middle of a line of verse (often marked by punctuation or natural syntactic break, as in Pope's "To err is human; || to forgive, divine") is called a:
e:
A Caesura (marked `||`) is an internal pause within a poetic line.
Enjambment (run-on line) is the opposite—when a sentence runs over from one line into the next without a terminal pause.

q: In his famous December 1817 letter to his brothers George and Tom, John Keats defined "Negative Capability" as the capacity of being in:
o: "uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason"
"total moral certainty guided by Neoclassical decorum"
"a state of intense political activism and revolutionary zeal"
"strict adherence to autobiographical confession in every lyric"
e: Keats cited William Shakespeare as the supreme possessor of Negative Capability—the artistic openness to mystery and empathy without forcing dogmatic rational closure (contrasting him with Coleridge).

q: Which of the following pairs of Shakespearean plays and their key literary sources is NOT correctly matched?
e: Statement D is NOT correctly matched: Plutarch's *Parallel Lives* (translated by Sir Thomas North) was the primary source for Shakespeare's ROMAN plays (*Julius Caesar*, *Antony and Cleopatra*, *Coriolanus*), whereas *The Tempest* has no single narrative source (drawing loosely on William Strachey's Bermuda shipwreck letter).

q: In which play does Shakespeare include the play-within-a-play titled *The Mousetrap* (originally *The Murder of Gonzago*) to "catch the conscience of the King"?
e:
In *Hamlet* (Act III, Scene 2), Hamlet stages *The Mousetrap* before Claudius to verify the Ghost's accusation of fratricide.
*A Midsummer Night's Dream* features the comic play-within-a-play *Pyramus and Thisbe* performed by the Mechanicals.

q: Which dramatic poem by John Milton (published in 1671 alongside *Paradise Regained*) is modelled strictly on Classical Greek tragedy (complete with Chorus and the Three Unities) and dramatizes the final day of a blinded biblical hero?
e:
*Samson Agonistes* (1671, a closet drama never meant for the stage) portrays the blind, captive Samson pulling down the Philistine temple of Dagon, echoing Milton's own blindness and political defeat after the 1660 Restoration.
*Comus* (1634) is a Masque celebrating chastity.

q: In Book I of *Paradise Lost*, who is the architect angel who built Pandemonium (the high capital of Satan and his peers in Hell)?
e:
Mulciber (identified with the Greek god Hephaestus / Roman Vulcan) designed Pandemonium in Book I of *Paradise Lost*.
Beelzebub is Satan's chief lieutenant; Moloch advocates open war; Belial argues for slothful peace; Mammon prefers mining Hell's riches.

q: In which year did William Wordsworth succeed Robert Southey as Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom, holding the post until his death in 1850?
e:
Wordsworth accepted the Poet Laureateship in 1843 (after initially declining due to age, accepting only on Prime Minister Robert Peel's assurance that no official court verse would be demanded).
Alfred, Lord Tennyson succeeded Wordsworth as Poet Laureate in 1850.

q: Which radical critic and essayist called Wordsworth a "Lost Leader" in a famous poem ("Just for a handful of silver he left us"), lamenting Wordsworth's shift from youthful revolutionary sympathy to late-life conservatism?
e:
Robert Browning wrote *The Lost Leader* (1845) criticizing Wordsworth's political conservatism and acceptance of a government pension/laureateship.
(Note: Shelley also wrote a sonnet *To Wordsworth* lamenting his political shift, while *The Lost Leader* is specifically Browning's.)

q: John Keats's haunting medieval ballad *La Belle Dame sans Merci* (1819) uses a distinctive four-line stanza pattern (abcb) whose FOURTH line is noticeably shortened to:
o: Two or three stressed beats (dimeter/trimeter), creating an eerie, abrupt silence
e: In *La Belle Dame sans Merci*, the first three lines of each quatrain are iambic tetrameter while the fourth line truncates sharply to four or five syllables (two/three stresses, e.g., "And no birds sing"), evoking desolation and enchantment.

q: Which Victorian poet-critic famously praised John Keats by writing "He is; he is with Shakespeare" in his essay on Keats (*Essays in Criticism*, Second Series)?
e: Matthew Arnold declared "He is; he is with Shakespeare" in tribute to Keats's "natural magic" and poetic maturity despite dying at age 25 (in Rome, 1821; epitaph: "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water").

q: In John Galsworthy's play *Strife* (1909), the uncompromising clash between capital and labour at the Trenartha Tin Plate Works is embodied by which two stubborn antagonists?
o: John Anthony (Chairman) and David Roberts (Workers' leader)
Ferdinand De Levis and Captain Ronald Dancy
e:
*Strife* (1909) pits iron-willed company chairman John Anthony against militant strike leader David Roberts; tragically, both are broken and the final settlement mirrors the exact compromise terms proposed BEFORE the strike began.
Options B, C, and D name characters from *Justice*, *The Silver Box*, and *Loyalties* respectively.

q: Under what pseudonym did John Galsworthy publish his earliest four works of fiction—including *From the Four Winds* (1897) and *Jocelyn* (1898)—before using his own name in *The Island Pharisees* (1904)?
e:
Galsworthy used the pen name "John Sinjohn" (meaning "John, son of John") for his first four books before adopting his real name in *The Island Pharisees* (1904).
"Boz" was Charles Dickens; "Ellis Bell" was Emily Brontë.

q: In his celebrated 1946 essay *Politics and the English Language*, what is George Orwell's central argument about modern political prose?
o: Sloppy, euphemistic, and cliché-ridden language corrupts clear thought and is deliberately used to defend the indefensible
Political writers should rely heavily on Latinate jargon and passive voice to appear authoritative
English grammar must be replaced by a simplified artificial language like Newspeak
Literary metaphors should never be used in journalism
e: In *Politics and the English Language* (1946), Orwell argues that political language is "designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable" and lays down six practical rules for clear, concrete, active English prose.

q: Which autobiographical 1936 essay by George Orwell—drawn from his five years serving in the Indian Imperial Police in Burma—exposes how imperialism traps and dehumanizes the colonizer ("when the white man turns tyrant it is his own freedom that he destroys")?
e:
*Shooting an Elephant* (1936, set in Moulmein, Lower Burma) recounts how the narrator shoots a calm elephant solely to avoid looking foolish before a crowd of thousands—a devastating critique of British imperialism.
Orwell's 1938 memoir *Homage to Catalonia* chronicles his anti-fascist service in the Spanish Civil War.
